title: Summarize Types of Malware and Tools/Methods for Detection, Removal, and Prevention

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Malware questions are behavior-recognition problems. Identify what the threat does, then select the appropriate detection, response, recovery, or prevention method.
bullets: Malware types and their signature behaviors
Recovery, endpoint detection, managed response, and cross-layer detection
Antimalware, email, firewall, education, and reinstallation controls

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When malware behavior appears, identify the threat from its strongest clue, then choose a tool or method that matches where the threat is detected and how much trust remains in the system.
sections.callout: Recognize the behavior → detect or contain → remove or recover → prevent recurrence.

entries.title: Trojan
paragraphs: Pretends to be legitimate or desirable software while performing malicious activity. Its defining clue is deception rather than file infection.
entries.recognitionCue: Looks safe but is malicious → Trojan.

entries.title: Rootkit
paragraphs: Hides malicious activity while maintaining privileged access and may interfere deeply with the operating system.
entries.recognitionCue: Deep stealth and privileged persistence → rootkit.

entries.title: Fileless Malware
paragraphs: Operates largely in memory or abuses legitimate system tools instead of relying on a traditional malicious executable on disk.
entries.recognitionCue: Memory or legitimate utilities → fileless malware.

entries.title: Virus
paragraphs: Infects files or executable content and replicates when the infected content runs.

entries.title: Spyware
paragraphs: Secretly collects information about browsing, applications, behavior, or personal information.

entries.title: Keylogger
paragraphs: Records keystrokes and may capture usernames, passwords, messages, or financial information.
entries.recognitionCue: Every key typed is recorded → keylogger.

entries.title: Stalkerware
paragraphs: Secretly monitors another person's activities, location, communications, or device and is associated with privacy abuse.

entries.title: Ransomware
paragraphs: Locks a system or encrypts files and demands payment to restore access.
entries.recognitionCue: Unreadable files plus a payment demand → ransomware.

entries.title: Boot Sector Virus
paragraphs: Infects boot-related storage areas and can execute during startup before normal OS operation.
entries.recognitionCue: Boot process infection → boot sector virus.

entries.title: Cryptominer
paragraphs: Steals CPU or GPU resources to generate cryptocurrency for an attacker, often causing high utilization, heat, fan activity, slowness, and power use.
entries.recognitionCue: Idle PC with a pegged CPU or GPU → cryptominer.

sections.title: Adware and Potentially Unwanted Programs

entries.title: Adware
paragraphs: Displays unwanted advertisements, pop-ups, or redirects.

entries.title: Potentially Unwanted Program (PUP)
paragraphs: Software that may not meet a strict malware definition but is unwanted or risky, such as bundled browser tools or questionable utilities.

sections.callout: Adware describes advertising behavior; PUP is the broader category of undesirable software.

table.caption: Behavior-to-malware matching
rows: Runs in memory or through legitimate tools

sections.title: Recovery Console
paragraphs: A recovery console or environment lets a technician diagnose and repair an operating system outside normal operation. It is useful when malware or corruption prevents normal startup.
sections.callout: The OS cannot operate normally → use a recovery environment.

sections.title: Tools and Methods: EDR, MDR, and XDR

entries.title: Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR)
paragraphs: Collects endpoint telemetry, detects suspicious behavior, and supports investigation and response on workstations, laptops, and servers.

entries.title: Managed Detection and Response (MDR)
paragraphs: Provides monitoring and response as a managed service, commonly through an outside security provider.
entries.recognitionCue: Outsourced security monitoring and response → MDR.

entries.title: Extended Detection and Response (XDR)
paragraphs: Correlates detections across multiple sources such as endpoints, email, identity, networks, and cloud services.

sections.title: Antivirus and Anti-Malware

entries.title: Antivirus
paragraphs: Detects and removes malicious software, historically emphasizing viruses and known signatures.

entries.title: Anti-Malware
paragraphs: Detects and removes a broader range of malicious software. Modern antivirus and anti-malware capabilities often overlap.

sections.callout: For the exam, antivirus is the traditional term; anti-malware emphasizes broader malicious-software protection.

entries.title: Email Security Gateway
paragraphs: Inspects email for malicious attachments, phishing, spam, and suspicious links before they reach users.
entries.recognitionCue: Stop a malicious attachment before the inbox → email security gateway.

entries.title: Software Firewalls
paragraphs: Run on an endpoint and control its network traffic to reduce exposure to unauthorized connections.

entries.title: User Education Regarding Common Threats
paragraphs: Teaches users to recognize suspicious links, attachments, downloads, software, and social-engineering techniques.

entries.title: Antiphishing Training
paragraphs: Focuses on urgency, impersonation, credential requests, suspicious links, and unusual attachments in fraudulent messages.
entries.recognitionCue: Teach users to spot fraudulent messages → antiphishing training.

sections.title: OS Reinstallation
paragraphs: If malware deeply compromises system integrity, a rootkit persists, or successful removal cannot be verified, reinstalling the operating system can restore a known-clean starting point.
bullets: Use reinstallation when confidence in ordinary cleanup is insufficient.
sections.callout: Cannot trust the system → rebuild it.

entries.title: Detect
paragraphs: Use antivirus, anti-malware, EDR, XDR, and email security gateways to identify suspicious or malicious activity.

entries.title: Respond and Remove
paragraphs: Use endpoint response tools, a recovery console, malware-removal tools, or OS reinstallation when integrity cannot be restored confidently.

entries.title: Prevent
paragraphs: Keep security tools updated, filter network and email traffic, and train users against common threats and phishing.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Repair outside normal boot → recovery console
Filter threats before inbox → email security gateway
System cannot be trusted → OS reinstallation

sections.title: Objective 2.4 Exam Trap
bullets: A Trojan relies on disguise; a virus infects and replicates.
Spyware broadly monitors; a keylogger specifically records keys; stalkerware covertly tracks a person.
A rootkit hides deeply with privilege; fileless malware operates largely without a traditional disk file.
Ransomware demands payment for access; a cryptominer quietly consumes compute resources.
Adware emphasizes advertisements; PUP is a broader unwanted-software category.
EDR is endpoint focused, MDR is a managed service, and XDR spans security sources.
Antivirus or anti-malware protects the endpoint; an email security gateway filters malicious mail before delivery.
If cleanup cannot restore trust, OS reinstallation may be the safest choice.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Dangerous email filtering → email security gateway
sections.callout: Recognize → detect → remove or recover → prevent.
